title: The Embarrassing T-Shirt
text:
In 2000 Thomas Gilovich, Victoria Husted Medvec and Kenneth Savitsky of Cornell University published a study that many people find reassuring. Each participant was asked to put on a T-shirt with a large picture of the singer Barry Manilow, a choice that the students at the time considered deeply embarrassing. The participant was then sent into a room where several other students were already sitting and filling out questionnaires.

After a short time the participant was led out again and asked to estimate how many of the people in the room had noticed who was on the shirt. Participants guessed that about half of them had. When the researchers asked the people in the room, only about a quarter could say who was on the shirt.

In other studies, people similarly overestimated how much others noticed their contributions and mistakes in a group discussion. The researchers called this the spotlight effect. Because we are so keenly aware of our own appearance and actions, we assume others are watching them just as closely. In fact, other people are mostly busy with their own concerns, and our slips, bad hair days and awkward moments are far less visible than they feel.
lesson: Far fewer people notice your awkward moments than you think. Worry less about how you look in a moment, and act more freely.
people: Thomas Gilovich, Victoria Husted Medvec, Kenneth Savitsky
source: Gilovich, T., Medvec, V. H., and Savitsky, K. (2000). The spotlight effect in social judgment: An egocentric bias in estimates of the salience of one's own actions and appearance. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 78(2), 211-222.
